text: Most of the inbox is cleared, and the only open window is the spreadsheet I finished twenty minutes ago. I stretch both arms over my head until my shoulders crack, then pour the last of the cold coffee into the sink. The printer down the hall whirs once and goes quiet. Nothing on the screen asks for me right now.

At four o'clock the team leaves the meeting room with its chairs pushed in and the whiteboard wiped clean. I walk past the kitchen where someone has left a bowl of clementines, and I take one, peeling it in one long strip. The window beside my desk shows the parking lot going gold in the low sun. My next task can wait until morning.

Finally the quarterly numbers balance to the penny, so I close the laptop lid and leave the charger coiled on the desk. Down in the lobby the security guard is reading a paperback behind the glass. I say goodnight to him, and he lifts his hand without looking up. Outside, the bus shelter has one bench free, and I sit on it for a while watching the streetlights blink on.

There is a stack of forms on the tray, and for once I am not counting them. I sign the last page with a blue pen, and the ink dries fast on the cheap paper. Through the open door I can hear the copier warming up and a colleague humming an old song. I slide my chair back an inch and lean into the rest of the afternoon.

Bread has come out of the oven with a crackling crust, and I tear the end off while it is still too hot to hold. I eat it standing at the counter over a sink full of bowls. Butter melts into the torn edge and runs down my wrist, so I lick it off. Half a loaf is left under the cloth, and I leave it there.

Peaches are in season, so I cut three of them over the sink and let the juice run down to my elbows. I eat the first slice leaning against the fridge with the door open for a second too long. The cold air moves over my bare feet. The second slice goes to the dog, who has been sitting at my knee since I took out the knife.

Across the long table on the back porch, my father is still telling the story about the ferry, and my cousin is refilling the water jug without being asked. The rice has gone cold in its bowl, and nobody minds. I take the last green bean from the platter, chew it slowly, and look at the plates pushed toward the middle. Dessert can come later.

Rain taps the skylight while I stand at the stove stirring a pan of oats with cinnamon. I pour milk in slowly and watch the surface turn from pale to cream. The kettle clicks off in the next room, and I leave it there. When I finally sit down, the bowl is exactly warm enough to hold in both hands.

Past the tunnel mouth, the train pulls into daylight, and the river appears on my left, flat and silver. I have a paper cup of tea balanced on my knee. Nobody across the aisle is talking, and a child two rows up is drawing with crayons on the back of a timetable. The next stop is twelve minutes away, and I am in no hurry to reach it.

Traffic on the ring road has slowed to a crawl, so I turn the radio off and let the engine idle. The sun is low and hits the windscreen at an angle that turns the dust into little sparks. I roll the window down an inch and smell cut grass from the verge. When the lane finally moves, I move with it, one car length at a time.

My bicycle ticks as it cools in the bike rack outside the library. I have ridden the long way along the canal, past the ducks and the rowers and the man selling roasted chestnuts from a cart. My legs feel loose and warm. I wheel the bike home slowly, letting the chain hang quiet, and I do not take the shortcut.

Nearly empty this late, the bus has its heater turned high. I sit by the window with my wet boots resting on the rubber mat, and nobody comes to tell me to move them. Sleet streaks the glass in thin lines. Two stops from home, I fold my hands in my lap and watch the wipers do their slow work.

Up the path the air shifts from warm resin to cold stream water every few steps. I stop on a flat rock above the pool and slip off my pack. Water slides over the stones in one steady sheet. I unwrap a block of cheese and a squashed sandwich and eat them slowly while a dragonfly hovers over the surface.

Below the ridge the valley is filling with evening, and the farms are turning into small squares of lamplight. I sit on the cold wall with my back to a birch trunk. A cow lows once somewhere below me, and an owl answers from the trees. The last of the light rests on the top of the hill, then slides off.

Frost still whitens the north side of the field when I start walking, but the sun clears the hedge within minutes. I follow the hedgerow with my hands jammed in my pockets. Every oak along it wears its own cap of lichen, pale green and rust. At the gate, I stop and watch a hare cross the stubble without hurrying.

Beneath the footbridge, a stream runs over flat stones, and the water is so clear I can count the pebbles. I crouch on the damp bank and dip two fingers in. The cold makes my knuckles ache, then goes numb. Upstream, a heron stands perfectly still, and I stay put too, watching it.

Long wet stripes shine across the kitchen floor where the mop has passed, catching the afternoon light. I drag the bucket to the back door and tip the grey water into the drain. I hang the cloth over the tap, then walk barefoot across the tiles and feel them cool under my soles.

Laundry comes out of the dryer warm and tangled, and I fold each towel into a neat square on the bed. The sheets smell faintly of outdoors. I stack them on the chest in the hall, the newest on top. The basket is empty now, and I leave it by the radiator where the cat can use it.

Under the hum of the dishwasher, I wipe the counters in slow circles. A crumb of sugar sticks to my thumb. I rinse the sponge until the water runs clear, wring it out, and set it on its ridge to dry. The window above the sink has steamed up at the corners.

I sweep the front step in the early dusk, pushing a little pile of leaves toward the gutter. The broom bristles scrape the concrete in a steady rhythm. When the last leaf goes over the edge, I lean the broom against the door frame and look at the swept step. The porch light clicks on above me.

A nurse wraps the cuff around my arm and pumps it up until it squeezes gently. The numbers come back lower than last month, and she writes them on the chart. I roll my sleeve down and do up the button. Outside the window, a bus idles at the kerb, its doors open and waiting.

Behind a closed curtain, the doctor listens to my chest with the cold disc and asks me to breathe in, then out, then in again. Her pen scratches a short line on the page. She tells me the results will come by letter, and there is nothing else on her list today. I pull my coat back on and zip it up slowly.

I lift my left leg one inch off the table, then another, then another. My hamstring pulls, and I breathe into it the way she showed me. The radio in the corner plays a station with no adverts. When she says that is enough for today, I sit up and rub my knee.

A paper pharmacy bag is light in my hand, with a leaflet folded inside and a receipt tucked into the top. I walk past the plant display and out into the car park. The afternoon is mild, and the pavement is dry. I swallow the first tablet with a sip of water from my bottle, right there on the bench.

Asleep on the sofa with her shoes still on, my sister has dozed off halfway through a film that is playing to nobody. I pull the blanket from the back of the chair and drape it over her feet. Outside, a car alarm goes off and then stops. I switch off the lamp and leave the hall light on for her.

Ruth is teaching her toddler to blow bubbles on the back step, and the wand keeps dripping onto her trainers. I hold the jar steady while she dips the loop. The bubbles drift over the hedge and pop one by one. Nobody needs to go anywhere until the jar is empty.

Grandma is shelling peas into a colander on the kitchen table, and I sit beside her with a bowl for the empty pods. Neither of us talks much. The radio murmurs the weather, and a bee bumps against the window. Each pod splits with a small crack, and the peas drop into the metal with a click.

Over the fence, my neighbour waves while he drags a hose across his lawn, and I wave back with a trowel in my hand. He and I stand there for a minute, talking about nothing much: the rain that is due, the plum tree that gave too much fruit. Then I kneel back down by the seedlings I was weeding.

Quiet except for a page turning now and then, the reading room hums around me, and the radiator ticks under the window. I have worked through three chapters without once looking up. My notes sit in neat columns, and the highlighter has dried out in my hand.

A bell rings at the end of the lesson, and the classroom empties in a rush of scraping chairs. I stay behind to finish one more sum on the board. Dust from the chalk drifts through a bar of sunlight. When the last pupil has gone, I rub the board clean with a wet sponge and see no reason to hurry.

Flashcards are fanned across the desk by the window, each one with a word in my messy handwriting. I shuffle them, turn one over, and say the answer out loud before I check it. Most are right. The kettle in the next room has boiled and gone quiet, and the mug beside me is still full.

Only twenty minutes remain on the clock above the exam hall door. I have read the last question twice and answered it in pencil. I set my pen down, square it with the edge of the paper, and look out at the playing field where a few boys are kicking a ball around.

At this hour the pool is nearly empty, and the lane ropes sway gently with each length I finish. My arms cut through the water, my breath comes in steady bursts, and the tiles slide past beneath me. At the wall I push off again straight away.

Along the towpath, I jog the last kilometre as the sky fades to pale orange. My trainers slap the packed gravel, and my shirt sticks to my back. A man on a bike rings his bell as he passes. At the gate I slow to a walk, bend over with my hands on my knees, and let my breath come back.

Rolled under my arm, the mat is still warm from the last class, and the studio smells faintly of eucalyptus. The teacher dims the lights, and the class sinks into the last long stretch. My spine lengthens, my shoulders drop away from my ears, and the room hums with breathing. When I stand up, I notice how light my feet feel.

The blue holds are worn smooth where others have gripped them, and chalk clings to my fingers. I reach for the next hold, shift my weight onto my right foot, and pull up one more move. From the top I can see the harbour and the cranes. I lower myself down slowly, hand over hand, and rest against the wall.

The wobbly table leg takes the new wedge with a solid tap, and I lean on the table to test it. It holds. I brush the sawdust off my hands onto my jeans and look at the pencil marks on the workbench. Evening light comes through the open garage door.

I sand the edge of the shelf in long, even strokes, blowing the pale dust off every few passes. The grain shows up warm and honey-coloured. I run my palm along the wood and find no rough spots left. My radio plays an old record, and the hours go by without me checking them.

Needles click as I work the last row of the scarf, the blue wool soft in my lap. I count stitches under my breath and do not lose my place once. When I bind off and snip the yarn, the scarf lies flat across my knees. I hold it up to the lamp and check the edges, and they are even all the way along.

Clay spins under my wet hands, rising into a neat cylinder with a steady hum. I dip my fingers in water, press down gently, and watch the rim straighten. Three finished bowls sit drying on the shelf behind me. I trim the base with a wire loop and leave the bowl where it sits.

Crates of leeks and late apples crowd the front table at the greengrocer's, and the man weighs my potatoes on an old brass scale. He drops in a single extra onion without comment. I carry the paper bag against my hip, its handles cutting a little into my fingers. I walk home the long way, past the bakery and the chemist.

A queue at the post office moves slowly, so I read the notices pinned to the board by the door. A stray dog sleeps under the bench outside. When my turn comes, I slide the parcel across the counter, sign the slip, and take a receipt with a torn corner. The street is bright and still.

Hardware shops smell of oil and cut keys. I find the right size of washer in a little plastic tray, check it against the sample in my palm, and take two more for good measure. The shopkeeper rings them up and wraps them in brown paper. I put them in my coat pocket and head out.

The returns slot swallows my three books with a soft thud. I stand in the entrance for a moment, breathing in the smell of old paper and radiator dust. Then I pick a fresh novel from the display table, tuck it under my arm, and step back out into the drizzle without rushing.

From the hotel window I watch the stallholders roll up their awnings one by one over the market. I drink coffee from a thin china cup and follow a cart of oranges as it creaks past the kiosk. The city map sits folded on the table, unopened. Today I have no plans to consult it.

Leaving the harbour, the ferry rocks gently, and gulls wheel above the wake. I stand at the rail with my collar up and watch the town shrink into a smudge of white houses. Spray hits my cheek now and then. The engine drones on, and I let the crossing take as long as it takes.

Vineyards bend along the hillsides as the mountain train climbs slowly through the valley. Across from me a woman dozes with her hat tipped over her eyes, and her head rocks in time with the wheels. Each village has its own bell tower. I keep my bag on my lap and look out until the last light fades over the lake.

Creaky floorboards greet me in the guesthouse room, where a window opens onto a courtyard full of geraniums. I unpack one shirt, two pairs of socks, and a paperback I have already read twice. The shower runs hot after one minute. I sit on the bed and listen to the church bell ring six.

Afternoon light falls across the piano keys in a warm stripe. I play the same four bars again, slower this time, letting each chord ring out before the next. The notes hang in the room a little longer than I expect. When I lift my hands, the silence sounds full.

A dab of ultramarine goes onto my brush, then swirls across the wet paper in a loose wash. The sky on the page is taking shape as the colour spreads and softens at the edges. I tip the board so a bead of water runs down, and I watch it bend the blue into a pale band near the horizon.

The guitar rests across my knee while I strum a slow progression I learned last spring. A few strings are slightly out of tune, but I leave them as they are. The cat from downstairs settles on the windowsill, tail curled, and listens too. The song loops back to the start, and I keep going.

Willow strips soak in a bucket by the door while I weave the basket's base. Each strip goes over and under the last, pulled snug with a gentle tug. The base is nearly round now, and the wicker smells green and damp. I set the next strip in place and press it down with my thumb.

A laptop screen glows softly in the dim room, and the last file uploads with a progress bar that fills to the end. I close the lid without shutting anything down. On my phone a message from home says the rain has stopped, and I type back one thumbs-up. Then I set the phone face down on the arm of the chair.

My brother's photo arrives by email while I dry the last mug, the one with the chipped handle. It shows his new kitten asleep on a folded sweater. I save the picture to the folder with the others and close the window. Nothing else in my email needs an answer tonight.

Photos finally sync to the laptop, and the thumbnails line up in a neat grid across the screen. I scroll once through the summer album, stopping at a blurry picture of a sea wall. I rename the folder, drag it onto the drive, and watch the bar creep to the end. Then I push the chair back from the desk.

An old tablet takes its time waking up, then shows the photo I set as the background years ago: a dock at dawn with the boats still tied up. I drag a few apps into a folder, delete the ones I no longer use, and check the battery. It has eighty percent left, which is more than I need.
